usamo-usamo-1973-01.title: Project onto the opposite face
usamo-usamo-1973-01.body:
Take the edge length to be $1$ and work with vectors from $A$: let $\vec b, \vec c, \vec d$ be the vectors $\vec{AB}, \vec{AC}, \vec{AD}$. They are unit vectors with pairwise dot products $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$.

**Step 1: project to the face $BCD$.** An interior point is $P = \alpha A + \beta B + \gamma C + \delta D$ with all coefficients positive and summing to $1$. Then $P' = \frac{\beta B+\gamma C+\delta D}{\beta+\gamma+\delta}$ lies in the interior of triangle $BCD$, and $P$ lies on segment $AP'$. Similarly define $Q'$. So $\angle PAQ = \angle P'AQ'$. If $P' = Q'$ the angle is $0$ and we are done, so assume $P'\neq Q'$.

**Step 2: extend to the boundary.** The line $P'Q'$ meets the boundary of triangle $BCD$ in two points $U$ and $V$, in the order $U, P', Q', V$ along the line, with $U\ne P'$ and $Q'\ne V$ because $P', Q'$ are interior points. Since $A$ is not on this line, the rays from $A$ to points of segment $UV$ sweep the angle $UAV$ monotonically, so
$$\angle UAV = \angle UAP' + \angle P'AQ' + \angle Q'AV > \angle P'AQ'.$$

**Step 3: $\angle UAV \le 60^\circ$.**
*Case 1: $U, V$ on the same side*, say $BC$. Then by the same additivity, $\angle UAV \le \angle BAC = 60^\circ$.

*Case 2: $U, V$ on different sides.* Two sides of a triangle share a vertex; by symmetry say $U \in BC$, $V\in BD$:
$$\vec{AU} = (1-\lambda)\vec b + \lambda \vec c, \qquad \vec{AV} = (1-\mu)\vec b + \mu\vec d, \qquad \lambda,\mu\in[0,1].$$
Using $|\vec b|=|\vec c|=|\vec d|=1$ and the dot products $\tfrac12$:
$$\vec{AU}\cdot\vec{AV} = (1-\lambda)(1-\mu) + \tfrac12\big[(1-\lambda)\mu + \lambda(1-\mu) + \lambda\mu\big] = \tfrac12\big(1 + (1-\lambda)(1-\mu)\big),$$
$$|AU|^2 = (1-\lambda)^2+\lambda^2+\lambda(1-\lambda) = 1-\lambda+\lambda^2,\qquad |AV|^2 = 1-\mu+\mu^2.$$
By AM–GM,
$$|AU|\,|AV| \le \tfrac12\big(|AU|^2+|AV|^2\big) = 1 - \tfrac{\lambda+\mu}2 + \tfrac{\lambda^2+\mu^2}2.$$
We claim this is at most $2\,\vec{AU}\cdot\vec{AV} = 2 - \lambda - \mu + \lambda\mu$. The difference is
$$\big(2-\lambda-\mu+\lambda\mu\big) - \Big(1 - \tfrac{\lambda+\mu}2 + \tfrac{\lambda^2+\mu^2}2\Big) = 1 - \tfrac{\lambda+\mu}{2} - \tfrac{(\lambda-\mu)^2}{2}.$$
WLOG $\lambda \ge \mu$; with $\delta = \lambda - \mu\in[0,1]$ we have $\delta^2\le\delta$, so $\tfrac{\lambda+\mu}2 + \tfrac{\delta^2}{2} \le \tfrac{\lambda+\mu}{2} + \tfrac{\lambda-\mu}{2} = \lambda \le 1$. Hence the difference is $\ge 0$ and
$$\cos\angle UAV = \frac{\vec{AU}\cdot\vec{AV}}{|AU|\,|AV|} \ge \frac12, \qquad\text{so } \angle UAV \le 60^\circ.$$

**Conclusion.** $\angle PAQ = \angle P'AQ' < \angle UAV \le 60^\circ$. ∎

usamo-usamo-1973-02.title: Work modulo 8
usamo-usamo-1973-02.body:
**The $X$ sequence.** $X_2 = 3$, $X_3 = 5$. If $(X_{n-1}, X_n) \equiv (3,5) \pmod 8$ then $X_{n+1} \equiv 5 + 6 = 11 \equiv 3$, and if $(X_{n-1},X_n)\equiv(5,3)$ then $X_{n+1}\equiv 3+10 = 13\equiv 5$. By induction, for $n \ge 2$ the residues alternate $3, 5, 3, 5, \dots$; in particular $X_n \equiv 3$ or $5 \pmod 8$ for all $n\ge2$.

**The $Y$ sequence.** $Y_0 = 1$, $Y_1 = 7$. If $(Y_{n-1},Y_n)\equiv(1,7)$ then $Y_{n+1}\equiv 14+3 = 17\equiv 1$, and if $(Y_{n-1},Y_n)\equiv(7,1)$ then $Y_{n+1}\equiv 2+21 = 23\equiv 7$. So $Y_n\equiv 1$ or $7\pmod 8$ for all $n$.

Hence $X_m \ne Y_n$ whenever $m \ge 2$. The remaining $X$-terms are $X_0 = X_1 = 1$. Since all terms of $Y$ are positive, $Y_{n+1} = 2Y_n + 3Y_{n-1} > Y_n$, so $Y$ is strictly increasing and $Y_n = 1$ only for $n = 0$. Therefore the only common value is $1$. ∎

usamo-usamo-1973-03.title: Count the triangles that miss the center
usamo-usamo-1973-03.body:
Label the vertices $0,1,\dots,2n$ around the circumcircle (center $O$). For a chosen triangle, going around the circle, the three chosen vertices split the $2n+1$ steps into gaps $g_1+g_2+g_3 = 2n+1$, each $g_i\ge1$.

**When is $O$ inside?** An inscribed triangle contains the circumcenter in its interior iff it is acute. The angle at a vertex equals half the central angle of the opposite arc, i.e. $\frac12\cdot \frac{2\pi g}{2n+1} = \frac{\pi g}{2n+1}$ for the gap $g$ opposite it. This is $<\frac\pi2$ iff $g < n + \tfrac12$, i.e. $g\le n$; it is never exactly $\frac\pi2$. So $O$ is inside iff all three gaps are $\le n$.

**Count the bad triangles.** Two gaps cannot both be $\ge n+1$ (their sum would exceed $2n+1$), so a bad triangle has exactly one gap $\ge n+1$. Let $v$ be the chosen vertex at the clockwise end of that gap; then the other two chosen vertices lie among the $n$ vertices following $v$ clockwise. Conversely, choosing any $v$ ($2n+1$ ways) and any $2$ of the next $n$ vertices ($\binom n2$ ways) leaves a gap of at least $2n+1-n = n+1$ back to $v$, and $v$ is determined by the triangle. So there are $(2n+1)\binom n2$ bad triangles.

**Probability.**
$$1 - \frac{(2n+1)\binom n2}{\binom{2n+1}3} = 1 - \frac{(2n+1)\,n(n-1)/2}{(2n+1)(2n)(2n-1)/6} = 1 - \frac{3(n-1)}{2(2n-1)} = \frac{n+1}{4n-2}.$$
(Check: $n = 1$ gives $1$, the triangle itself; $n=2$ gives $\tfrac12$: in a regular pentagon 5 of the 10 triangles contain the center.)

**Answer:** $\dfrac{n+1}{4n-2}$.

usamo-usamo-1973-04.title: Elementary symmetric functions
usamo-usamo-1973-04.body:
Let $e_1 = x+y+z$, $e_2 = xy+yz+zx$, $e_3 = xyz$. Then $e_1 = 3$ and
$$e_2 = \frac{e_1^2 - (x^2+y^2+z^2)}{2} = \frac{9-3}{2} = 3.$$
Newton's identity $x^3+y^3+z^3 = e_1^3 - 3e_1e_2 + 3e_3$ gives $3 = 27 - 27 + 3e_3$, so $e_3 = 1$. Therefore $x,y,z$ are the three roots (with multiplicity) of
$$t^3 - e_1t^2 + e_2t - e_3 = t^3 - 3t^2 + 3t - 1 = (t-1)^3,$$
so $x = y = z = 1$, which indeed satisfies the system. **Answer:** $(x,y,z) = (1,1,1)$ only.

usamo-usamo-1973-04.title: Shift by 1
usamo-usamo-1973-04.body: Put $a = x-1$, $b = y-1$, $c = z-1$. The first equation gives $a+b+c = 0$. Then $x^2+y^2+z^2 = (a^2+b^2+c^2) + 2(a+b+c) + 3$, so $a^2+b^2+c^2 = 0$, and hence $ab+bc+ca = \frac{(a+b+c)^2 - (a^2+b^2+c^2)}2 = 0$. Similarly $x^3+y^3+z^3 = (a^3+b^3+c^3) + 3(a^2+b^2+c^2) + 3(a+b+c) + 3$, so $a^3+b^3+c^3 = 0$. Since $a^3+b^3+c^3 - 3abc = (a+b+c)(\dots) = 0$, also $abc = 0$. All elementary symmetric functions of $a,b,c$ vanish, so they are roots of $t^3$: $a=b=c=0$, i.e. $x=y=z=1$.

usamo-usamo-1973-05.title: Use $u+v+w=0 \Rightarrow u^3+v^3+w^3=3uvw$
usamo-usamo-1973-05.body:
Suppose $x = \sqrt[3]p$, $y = \sqrt[3]q$, $z = \sqrt[3]r$ ($p,q,r$ distinct primes) are terms of an arithmetic progression with difference $d$. Then $y - x = md$ and $z - x = nd$ for some integers $m, n$. As $x,y,z$ are distinct, $d \neq 0$, $m\ne 0$, $n\ne0$, $m\ne n$. Eliminating $d$: $n(y-x) = m(z-x)$, i.e.
$$(m-n)x + ny - mz = 0.$$
Put $u = (m-n)x$, $v = ny$, $w = -mz$. Then $u+v+w = 0$, and the identity
$$u^3+v^3+w^3 - 3uvw = (u+v+w)(u^2+v^2+w^2-uv-vw-wu)$$
gives $u^3+v^3+w^3 = 3uvw$, i.e.
$$(m-n)^3p + n^3q - m^3r = -3(m-n)nm\,\sqrt[3]{pqr}.$$
The left side is an integer and the coefficient $3(m-n)nm$ is a nonzero integer, so $\sqrt[3]{pqr}$ is rational.

But a rational cube root of a positive integer $N$ is an integer (if $(a/b)^3 = N$ in lowest terms, then $b^3 \mid a^3$, forcing $b = 1$), so $pqr$ would be a perfect cube. This is false: each of the primes $p, q, r$ divides $pqr$ exactly once, while in a cube every prime exponent is a multiple of $3$. Contradiction. ∎
